Relationships and flows

Source: vignettes/articles/relationships.Rmd
relationships.Rmd

Charts for the relationship between two numeric variables, and for flows between categories.

Chart Use it when
scatter_plot() You look at the relationship between two numeric variables, optionally by group, with bubbles or a trend line
hexbin_plot() A scatter plot has too many points to read
chord_diagram() You show flows between categories, such as migration or trade

scatter_plot()

A scatter plot shows how two numeric variables move together. Hover a point to read its values; drag a box to select points, then use Zoom to look closer (double-click resets the view).

scatter_plot(
  data = mpg,
  x = "displ",
  y = "hwy",
  x_title = "Engine displacement (litres)",
  y_title = "Highway miles per gallon",
  title = "Bigger engines, fewer miles"
)

Groups and trend lines

group colours the points by a column. The legend is interactive: click an entry to hide a group, double-click to keep only that group. trend = "lm" fits a linear regression per group, with its 95% confidence band; hover a line to read its slope, intercept and R².

scatter_plot(
  data = iris,
  x = "Sepal.Length",
  y = "Petal.Length",
  group = "Species",
  trend = "lm",
  title = "Petal and sepal length by species"
)

Bubbles, colour scales and labels

size_by maps a third variable to the point area. A numeric group gives a colour gradient. label names each point in the tooltip, and show_labels writes some of them on the chart (labels that would overlap are skipped). tooltip adds more columns to the tooltip, and trend = "loess" draws a smooth curve.

cars <- mtcars
cars$model <- rownames(mtcars)

scatter_plot(
  data = cars,
  x = "hp",
  y = "mpg",
  size_by = "disp",
  group = "qsec",
  label = "model",
  show_labels = c("Maserati Bora", "Toyota Corolla", "Lotus Europa", "Cadillac Fleetwood"),
  tooltip = c("cyl", "gear"),
  trend = "loess",
  title = "Horsepower and fuel economy",
  subtitle = "Bubble area: displacement. Colour: quarter-mile time (s)"
)

Log scales and reference lines

Skewed variables are easier to read on a log scale (x_scale, y_scale). h_lines and v_lines draw labelled reference lines.

states <- data.frame(
  state      = rownames(state.x77),
  region     = state.region,
  area       = state.x77[, "Area"],
  population = state.x77[, "Population"],
  income     = state.x77[, "Income"]
)

scatter_plot(
  data = states,
  x = "area",
  y = "population",
  group = "region",
  label = "state",
  show_labels = TRUE,
  tooltip = "income",
  x_scale = "log",
  y_scale = "log",
  h_lines = c("Median population" = median(states$population)),
  x_title = "Area (square miles)",
  y_title = "Population (thousands, 1975)",
  title = "US states: area and population"
)

In Shiny

Inside a Shiny app, the chart reports what the user selects. With d3Output("cars"), input$cars_selected holds the row numbers of data inside the brushed box, and input$cars_clicked the row of the last clicked point:

output$cars <- renderD3(scatter_plot(mtcars, "wt", "mpg"))
output$picked <- renderTable(mtcars[input$cars_selected, ])

hexbin_plot()

hexbin_plot() is inspired by the hexbin transform of Observable Plot. It groups points into a grid of hexagons coloured by the number of observations in each one, which keeps dense scatter plots readable. The binning is written by hand, since d3-hexbin is not bundled with r2d3.

hexbin_plot(
  data     = faithful,
  x        = "waiting",
  y        = "eruptions",
  bin_width = 14,
  x_title   = "Waiting time to next eruption (min)",
  y_title   = "Eruption duration (min)",
  title    = "Old Faithful eruptions"
)

A log colour scale helps when counts are very skewed:

set.seed(1)
dsample <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 10000), ]

hexbin_plot(
  data         = dsample,
  x            = "carat",
  y            = "price",
  bin_width     = 8,
  color_palette = "Viridis",
  color_scale   = "log",
  title        = "Diamond price by carat"
)

chord_diagram()

chord_diagram() shows the flows between a set of entities as outer arcs joined by ribbons. Its look and hover behaviour are inspired by the chord chart of Nivo: hovering over an entity fades every ribbon not connected to it, and clicking an arc pins the highlight.

migration <- data.frame(
  from  = c("Africa", "Africa", "Africa", "Asia", "Asia", "Asia",
            "Europe", "Europe", "Latin America", "Latin America",
            "North America", "Oceania", "Asia", "Europe"),
  to    = c("Europe", "North America", "Asia", "Europe", "North America",
            "Oceania", "North America", "Asia", "North America", "Europe",
            "Europe", "Asia", "Africa", "Oceania"),
  value = c(420, 150, 90, 610, 520, 230, 180, 120, 870, 260,
            95, 40, 60, 75)
)

chord_diagram(
  data        = migration,
  from        = "from",
  to          = "to",
  value       = "value",
  value_format = ",.0f",
  title       = "Migration flows between regions (illustrative data)"
)

A square matrix with dimnames works too:

hair <- matrix(
  c(11975,  5871, 8916, 2868,
     1951, 10048, 2060, 6171,
     8010, 16145, 8090, 8045,
     1013,   990,  940, 6907),
  nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("Black", "Blond", "Brown", "Red"),
                  c("Black", "Blond", "Brown", "Red"))
)

chord_diagram(
  data        = hair,
  colors      = c("#3b3b3b", "#f2c45a", "#8c5a3c", "#d0533a"),
  ribbon_color = "gradient",
  pad_angle    = 0.05,
  value_format = ",.0f",
  title       = "Hair color flows"
)
